teaching.causalExplanation: Start by organising the data. Each group gets its own column, with one value per cell, and a heading at the top so nobody mixes them up. The twelve bedroom values go in column B, and the eight elsewhere values in column C. Underneath, a summary block. Equals COUNT checks how many. Equals AVERAGE gives the mean. Equals MEDIAN, the median. Equals MAX minus MIN, the range. And equals STDEV dot P, the standard deviation. Write the five formulas for column B, then use the same formulas, pointed at column C. The bedroom group's mean is six point five eight hours, its median six point seven five, its range five point five, and its sigma one point three seven. The elsewhere group's are eight point one three, eight, two point five, and nought point seven eight. And if a value is wrong and gets fixed, every result updates by itself. Now compare. Start with the centre. Use the same measure for both groups. The elsewhere group's mean is eight point one three hours, against six point five eight. That's about one and a half hours more, on average. The medians agree, eight against six point seven five, so the extra sleep isn't just one or two big values. Quoting both, when they agree, makes the comparison stronger. Notice the pattern of the sentence. Which group, which way, and by how much. Comparing one group's mean with the other group's median would be a slip. They measure different things. Then compare the spread. The elsewhere group's sigma is nought point seven eight hours, against one point three seven for the bedroom group. Smaller spread means steadier sleep, so the elsewhere group's sleep is more consistent, typically within about three quarters of an hour of its mean. The bedroom group's sleep varies more, and its range, five and a half hours against two and a half, says the same. Part of that is the three hour night. One very short night widens the bedroom group's spread, and it pulls its mean down too. We'll measure exactly how much in a later video.
